editorialNotes.short: A suave, sensuous 1996 set from Vienna’s downtempo dons.
editorialNotes.standard: Despite a lengthy discography stretching back to the early ’90s, Kruder & Dorfmeister didn’t release their debut album until 2020. In the absence of a proper long-player, the Viennese duo’s 1998 remix collection, The K&D Sessions, served for years as a sort of proxy full-length debut. Two years before that, however, they put their name to the fourth installment of the DJ-Kicks series, where they sketched the outline of their trademark blend of downtempo, nu-jazz, and blunted soul. Despite drawing from more than a dozen different artists, the set flows as naturally as if it were all their own work. Highlighting artists like Ninja Tune staple The Herbaliser along with lesser-known producers like Small World and Tango, the opening stretch slips from laidback breakbeats into smooth, jazzy drum ’n’ bass; K&D ride that dual groove for a while, folding half-time head-nodders into double-speed rollers like Aquasky’s “Kauna.” The vibes reach a peak about halfway through, as Hardfloor’s acidic “Dadamnphreaknoizphunk? (Dubdope)” paves the way for Thievery Corporation’s now-classic “Shaolin Satellite,” which in turn sets the stage for Kruder & Dorfmeister’s “High Noon,” a Rhodes-kissed jam that sums up trip-hop at its most sensual. From there on out, it’s a captivating blend of soundtrack strings, dub delay, bossa nova guitars, and hip-hop scratching—which is to say, an all-encompassing snapshot of mid-’90s downtempo at its best.

editorialNotes.short: Dance music’s trickster DJ spins up a moon-eyed daydream of a set.
editorialNotes.standard: DJ Koze is one of the most inventive remixers out there, so it figures that his DJ-Kicks is less like one of his club sessions and more like an extended remix, swirling together exclusive edits of his chosen selections into a playfully sidewinding set that’s steeped in his quirky sensibility. (Where else are you going to encounter a William Shatner monologue in what is ostensibly a house-music set?) He draws as much from leftfield hip-hop as he does dance music—hence cuts early on from cLOUDDEAD, Mndsgn, and Freddie Gibbs & Madlib—and roams far and wide, stylistically. Broadcast’s “Tears in the Typing Pool” suggests a lost psychedelic-folk song from the ’60s; Daniel Lanois’ “Carla” dips a toe into pedal-steel exotica; and Marker Starling’s “In Stride” evokes vintage bedroom soul at its shaggiest. No matter the genre, the common denominators are juicy tone colors and lopsided beats, all threaded together with wistfully dreamlike vocals. Electronic music has rarely sounded so enchanting.

editorialNotes.short: Detroit’s deep house maestro spins a soulful, anything-goes set.
editorialNotes.standard: Thanks to classics like “I Can’t Kick This Feeling When It Hits” and “J.A.N.,” Detroit’s Moodymann is synonymous with some of the deepest house and techno ever set to tape. As a DJ, though, the artist otherwise known as Kenny Dixon Jr. ventures far beyond the four-to-the-floor guide rail. Across two gently mind-melting hours, Moodymann twists and turns his way through a staggering array of soul, funk, beat music, folk, synth-pop, and more. The opening tracks—featuring laidback soul and boom-bap from Cody ChesnuTT, Dopehead, and Jitwam—are a head-nodder’s delight; following a vibey stretch of Flying Lotus and Nightmares on Wax, he starts pulling out curveballs: Little Dragon’s wistful electro-pop, Andres’ Latin funk, even a vocoder-heavy jam from Caribou’s alias Les Sins. This being a Moodymann joint, Dixon himself supplies sly edits to many of his selections, guaranteeing that you’ll never hear these songs the same way anywhere else.

editorialNotes.short: The Canadian DJ connects ’80s disco-soul and deep house.
editorialNotes.standard: !K7’s long-running DJ-Kicks mix series has generally been the place for established legends—or legends in the making—of dance music to show off their one-of-a-kind skills as technicians and selectors. Jayda G—the London-based Canadian producer/DJ born Jayda Guy—uses the platform to do both while drawing a line between the richly orchestrated disco-soul and jazz-funk of the ’80s and the sleek deep house of today. “I wanted to showcase my more eclectic electronic music side,” she tells Apple Music of her mix, which moves from rare gems such as Aged in Harmony’s “You’re a Melody” and Light of the World’s “London Town” to premiering a number of brand-new tracks like DJ BORING’s “Gardenia,” Fred again..’s “Diana (You Don't Even Know),” and LNS’s “Bitumen.” "People may not hear those types of songs in my sets all the time, but they are tracks that I truly love,” she says of the dynamic tracklist. But whether it’s those languid songs that open or the more chugging percussion tunes that take it home, the through line here, not surprisingly, is a groove so wide and deep you could turn a cruise ship around in it.

editorialNotes.short: A percussive club set infused with the artist’s typical experimental spirit.
editorialNotes.standard: Laurel Halo is a restlessly experimental musician: Her curiosity has taken her from the electro-pop and vaporwave of her early work into avant techno, electro-acoustic music, film soundtracks, and collaborations with artists like Eli Keszler and Moritz von Oswald. What’s less documented is her facility for the leftfield club sounds she hinted at on a collaborative EP with Hodge on Livity Sound in 2018. But Halo’s DJ-Kicks, released the following year, makes for a deep dive into cutting-edge club rhythms where her long-standing interest in murky tones and tactile textures meets the heavyweight propulsion of bass music. She kicks off the set with a fake-out, smearing detuned piano chords across the spectrum and then plunging into a shape-shifting sequence of techno and electro. She has a knack for playing contrasting tracks off each other in surprising ways: The glancing chords of Parris’ spacious, dubby “Puro Rosaceaes” set up the dissonant spirals of Rrose’s “Cricoid Pressure”; the rolling breakbeat techno of Dario Zenker’s “Koraimer Bro” blasts open a hole for Final Cut’s “Temptation,” a seldom-heard 1989 song from Jeff Mills’ industrial project. Halo’s own productions are often notable for their subtlety, but here, the intensity just keeps building all the way to the end—at least until The Whitefield Brothers’ percussive “NTU” closes out the mix with a campfire drum circle, complete with chirping crickets. But then, it wouldn’t be a Laurel Halo project without one final curveball.

editorialNotes.short: The IDM veteran delivers an eye-opening set of leftfield club tracks.
editorialNotes.standard: As a longtime producer of ambient-tinged IDM, Gold Panda isn’t necessarily known as a DJ, which is precisely why his contribution to the DJ-Kicks series is such a revelation. Whereas you might expect to find him dealing principally in downbeat tempos and silky textures, he dives right in with a pulsing beat of his own creation, followed by deep house from Melchior & Pronsato, throbbing club rhythms from Bok Bok, and even the slinky-yet-forceful electro of Detroit icons Drexciya. A surprise lurks around every corner: A breakbeat cut from legendary dark-ambient musician Muslimgauze gives way to slinky dubstep from Ramadanman; trim minimalism from SND spills into Zomby’s 8-bit fantasias and on into a melancholy synth classic from Closer Musik. And on it goes like that, switchbacking from style to style while retaining a remarkably consistent mood of bright-eyed curiosity.

editorialNotes.short: The Berlin-based star selects tracks for the esteemed mix series.
editorialNotes.standard: For the 69th installment of !K7’s DJ-Kicks mix series, the Berlin independent label tapped dance music superstar Peggy Gou. A native of South Korea who now lives in Germany, the inventive DJ/producer is known for exquisitely curated live sets that offer a global perspective, sampling a range of eras and regions from classic Chicago house to playful nu disco. In recent years, she began releasing her own sultry productions which feature her featherweight vocals over growling grooves (listen to "It Makes You Forget [Itgehane]” for a taste). But her DJ-Kicks mix is less an impression of her live sets and more a musical diary, showcasing a selection of songs that have shaped her identity. Again, she casts a wide net: There’s dizzying polyrhythmic experimentations (Aphex Twin’s “Vordhosbn”), off-kilter electro (“Perseguido Por El Rayo” by Pegasus), and delirious, sputtering techno from Detroit’s Kyle Hall (“Flemmenup”).

editorialNotes.short: A legendary 1999 set from the star-crossed drum ’n' bass duo.
editorialNotes.standard: In a just world, Kemistry & Storm’s DJ-Kicks would have been just the first of many triumphs. The pioneering UK duo had gotten their start on London pirate radio in the early ’90s, two of the only women to rise to the top of the overwhelmingly masculine drum ’n’ bass scene; in 1994, with Goldie, they cofounded Metalheadz, perhaps the most iconic drum ’n’ bass label of all time. They were known mainly in the underground, but in 1999, the fledgling DJ-Kicks series tapped them for a set, making them the first junglists to helm a mix for the franchise. Released in January 1999, it marked their breakout moment, giving both them and the scene a major push into the spotlight. But just four months later, Kemistry was killed in a road accident while the duo was returning from a gig. Decades later, her absence remains acutely felt (Storm continues DJing while keeping the memory of her friend and partner alive). This record is a reminder of what made them so special. In 17 tracks, many of them from the Metalheadz catalog, they cut a winding path through dark, tech-y steppers (Dom & Roland’s “Trauma”), sun-kissed jazz (Sci-Clone’s “Everywhere I Go”), apocalyptic Amen workouts (Test’s “Static [K7 Mix]”), and boundary-breaking tracks that still sound futuristic today, like DJ Die’s “Clear Skyz” and Goldie’s “Hyaena.” A landmark set, it’s a tribute to their original vision and a melancholy suggestion of avenues they never got to explore.

editorialNotes.short: A breakbeat wizard blazes a blissful trail from jazz to jungle.
editorialNotes.standard: Under his own name, Paul Woolford is a remixer with an unerring crossover instinct—the man responsible for flipping songs from acts like Dua Lipa and Rag’n’Bone Man & P!nk into proper dance-floor fillers. But he’s built a parallel career keeping the underground legacy of breakbeat culture alive under his Special Request alias. Given that project’s immersion in classic jungle, his DJ-Kicks isn’t nearly as full-on as you might expect: He eases listeners in with an extended intro of cosmic jazz, lush NYC garage, and deep house. But halfway in, things take a turn toward techno as the laser zaps of Krystal Klear’s “Tun Valve” clear a path for Speedy J’s classic “De-Orbit” and AceMo’s lush, Detroit-inspired “Sequence of Life.” Only in the final stretch does Woolford open the floodgates for a rush of rolling jungle breaks—and when he does, it’s absolutely glorious, like a 747 lifting off above green, rolling hills against the most majestic orange sunset you’ve ever seen.

editorialNotes.short: A muscular, minimalist techno set from a Detroit icon.
editorialNotes.standard: On his first official mix since 2008’s Fabric 39, Robert Hood proves why he has remained one of Detroit techno’s most enduring DJs. Much like his own muscular, minimalist productions, which account for more than half the tracklisting, Hood’s mixing relentlessly hones in on the meat of the groove. From start to finish, the set toes a tightrope-narrow path of pinging synth sequences stretched taut above cavernous kicks. The energy starts off at peak time and stays there, but it’s never monotonous, thanks to careful pacing. It hits an early apex with Slam’s sleek, steely “Remain” and quickly inches higher with Marcel Fengler’s hammered-metal “Thwack,” but it’s never more thrilling than when Hood’s test-tone bleeps flash, which they do frequently—blaring alarms of a near-constant state of emergency.

editorialNotes.short: The drum ’n’ bass icon delves into the moody depths of his record collection.
editorialNotes.standard: Photek originally made his name in the mid-'90s with a dazzling strain of drum ’n’ bass marked by drums that flashed like a samurai’s blade. But despite the widespread impact of his stylistic innovations, Photek (aka Rupert Parkes) didn’t stay in one place for long: By 2000, he’d embraced deep, emotive house and techno, and he just kept on shape-shifting, experimenting with dubstep and then moving into video game and film soundtracks. His 2012 DJ-Kicks mix—incredibly, his first commercial mix album—captures the scope of his range. The set begins with a half-time stepper from his own hand, then sinks into slow-motion bass music and even, surprisingly, nu-disco. As the tempo rises, he touches on dark garage (Dustmite and KURU’s “Bare”), acid (his own “M25fm,” with Pinch), and even classic breakbeat techno (Baby Ford + EON’s “Dead Eye,” from 1994). The set’s middle stretch delves into deep, brooding tech house with cuts from Daze Maxim and Guy J & Miriam Vaga before Sepalcure’s “Taking You Back” brings us back to the types of slinky, shadowy bass music that dominated adventurous dance floors around the time Photek recorded the set. The set amounts to a fascinating tour of Parkes’ tastes—and a portrait that fans of his early work might never have guessed at.

editorialNotes.short: A reflective mix of heady techno and sleek, spiraling experimentations.
editorialNotes.standard: In this edition of German label !K7’s long-running electronic mix series, LA-based crate digger Avalon Emerson delivers a spiraling, introspective compilation that’s perfect for lockdown listening. The DJ/producer is known to infuse her hard-hitting techno sets with breaths of pop, but here, she reverse-engineers the formula: melody, vocals, and atmosphere take the lead while beats bubble up in the background. Emerson opens with her own cover of “Long Forgotten Fairytale,” the 1999 single by The Magnetic Fields, and makes it feel disco-fied and remarkably soulful, tangling her faint vocals with glimmering, neon synths. In a year when every pop star has released their own version of a Robyn dance-floor jam—“crying-in-the-club anthems,” or so they’re called—few have captured the all-together-now gloom that Emerson hits on here. Later on, she lifts out of her solitude for a few moments of release that come in leftfield disco streaks (Soundstream’s “3rd Movement”) and psychedelic funk bops (The Dirtbombs’ cover of A Number of Names’ “Sharevari”—the very DNA of Detroit techno), but the bliss is short-lived. This is 2020, a year of disorienting seclusion and fear—which is perhaps best expressed through her spiritual collaboration with Austra. “We’ll figure it out/We’ll figure it out/We’ll figure it out,” Katie Stelmanis sings in a choir-like echo. “But what if we don’t?”

editorialNotes.short: The UK DJ bends hip-hop, house, and jungle to his eclectic will.
editorialNotes.standard: Leon Vynehall made his mark as a producer by stretching house music’s conventions to accommodate, well, anything—avian mating rituals, say, or his grandparents’ migration from England to New York. His debut mix album ranges just as widely, collecting tracks old (Haruomi Hosono’s ’80s electro-pop, Bourbonese Qualk’s chilly industrial) and new (like exclusives from UK bass savant Ploy and rising house maven Peach), and taking the tempo from skulking hip-hop through skipping garage to full-on jungle. As much as a display of mixing prowess, it’s a snapshot of the UK DJ’s unusual thought process, making connections between moods that are dreamy and aggro, ethereal and paranoid, all with exceptional skill and enviable grace.

editorialNotes.short: A classic 2010 set that leaves dance music behind for points unknown.
editorialNotes.standard: James Holden has had one of the most unexpected trajectories in electronic music: Fresh out of adolescence, he got his start making trance music in the early 2000s, singlehandedly reshaped the minimal scene with his Border Community label, then more or less abandoned club music in favor of experimental fusion and electronic improv. Recorded in 2010, Holden’s DJ-Kicks mix neatly divides the “then” and “now” phases of his career: It’s largely laced by steadily thrumming 4/4 rhythms, yet it’s also psychedelic to the core, awash in spinning arpeggios and surging synths. Following an ambient intro from post-rockers Piano Magic, he dives into a succession of muscular grooves, folding punk-funk stomp and techno pulse into atmospheres reminiscent of Germany’s kosmische music of the ’70s. But with Mogwai’s throbbing “The Sun Smells Too Loud (Holden Remix),” the set’s orbit gradually grows wider and wobblier, taking in Kieran Hebden & Steve Reid’s laptop-assisted free jazz, Eric Copeland’s colorful shuffle, and Lucky Dragons’ minimalist gamelan. It all comes to a head with Holden’s lopsided “Triangle Folds,” exclusive to this set, before slipping sideways into a downright clubby finale of techno and acid. Taken together, the mix is a snapshot of one of electronic music’s most restless thinkers, capturing one eureka moment after another.

editorialNotes.short: The visionary Detroit producer offers a modern tour of his city.
editorialNotes.standard: Part of what makes Theo Parrish’s mixes so compelling is how effortlessly he manages to situate house in the broader galaxy of Black American music, from funk and jazz fusion to gospel and R&B. Framed as a showcase for underground Detroit, his contribution to !K7’s vaunted DJ mix series is unusual in that it’s the first time a DJ-Kicks set has focused almost entirely on exclusive tracks (the exception being Parrish and Duminie DePorres’ “The Real Deal”), not to mention by artists with almost no other credits to their names—a testament to Parrish’s community-first approach. Conscious rap (John C & Meftah’s “Full”), beat-tape abstractions (Donald Lee Roland II’s “Simba’s Theme”), piano-driven house (Specter’s “The Upper Room”)—the styles shift, but the mood is consistently introspective and uplifting. And like Parrish’s own productions, the beauty of them is how they balance their sophistication with a homespun, almost punk approach that serves as a reminder that the point isn’t perfecting—it’s doing.
